text: By default, S3 overwrites and deletes are permanent. This lesson covers the three features that change that: versioning, which protects against accidents; lifecycle rules, which automate aging data out; and the policy layers that decide who can touch a bucket at all.

Turning on versioning with put-bucket-versioning changes two behaviors at once. Every new PUT to an existing key now creates a brand-new version with its own version ID instead of erasing the old one, and a plain DELETE doesn't destroy anything — it just adds a delete marker on top.

That delete marker is the whole trick: the object appears gone in normal listings, but every prior version is still sitting there in the bucket. Recovering from an accidental delete, or an accidental overwrite, just means removing the marker or restoring a specific version ID — not restoring from some separate backup system.

A lifecycle rule automates what you'd otherwise have to remember to do by hand: transition objects to a cheaper storage class, or expire them outright, purely based on age. The example here moves anything under logs/ to Glacier after 30 days and deletes it after a year, and once it's applied, S3 enforces it on every matching object forever.

Access runs through two policy layers that both have to allow an action: a bucket policy, which is resource-based and travels with the bucket itself, and an IAM policy, which is identity-based and attached to the user or role making the request. The real danger is a bucket policy or legacy ACL written too broadly, granting public access by accident — one of the most common real-world causes of a cloud data leak.

S3 Block Public Access exists specifically to catch that mistake, overriding any policy or ACL that would otherwise expose a bucket publicly. With versioning, lifecycle rules, and access control covered, next up is EBS — the network-attached block storage that gives an EC2 instance its virtual hard drive.
